The experiments were conducted on a scaled-down model of a single-bladed H-type Darrieus wind turbine in a recirculating water channel.
The turbine blade had a NACA0018 profile, a chord length of 6 cm, and a span of 15 cm.
The turbine radius was 15 cm, yielding a chord-to-diameter ratio of 0.2.
The experiments were conducted at a Reynolds number of 50,000 based on the blade rotational velocity of 0.89 Hz.
The unsteady blade loads were measured using 20 strain gauges forming 5 full Wheatstone bridge channels on the blade shaft.
The Greenberg model was able to predict the maximum radial force coefficient during the upwind portion of the cycle even at the low tip-speed ratio of λ=1.5.

The Greenberg model failed to accurately predict the radial force coefficient during the downwind portion of the cycle, especially at low tip-speed ratios, due to the effects of flow separation and blade-wake interaction.
The Fourier series approximation with 8 terms was found sufficient to accurately fit the effective angle of attack and flow velocity variations for tip-speed ratios λ≥1.2.
The maximum radial force coefficient and its timing were well predicted by the Greenberg model for the higher tip-speed ratio of λ=4.5.
The Greenberg model does not account for the effects of dynamic stall and blade-wake interaction, which become important at low tip-speed ratios.

The proposed adaptation of the Greenberg model shows great potential for diagnosing regions of separated flow and quantifying the relative influences of dynamic stall and turbine kinematics on blade loading.
Future research can extend the method to model the loads on any airfoil undergoing arbitrary combinations of pitching, surging, and heaving motions.
The experiments were conducted in a recirculating water channel with a test section of 0.6m×0.6m×3m and a maximum flow velocity of 1 m/s.
The blade had a pitching axis located at the quarter-chord position, corresponding to a chord-normalized distance of d = -0.25.
The experimental data was phase-averaged over 100 cycles and conditioned using a low-pass filter with a cut-off frequency of 30 Hz.
